                            </HBox>
                        </l:content>
                    </l:VerticalLayout>
                </content>
            </Panel>

            <Panel headerText="Result" class="sapUiResponsiveMargin">
                <content>
                    <MessageStrip id="resultStrip" text="Run an operation above to see the result here." type="Information" showIcon="true" class="sapUiSmallMargin" />
                </content>
            </Panel>

        </content>
    </Page>
</mvc:View>

Step 9 – Connect the UI to the CAP Service

The controller uses fetch() to call the CAP OData V4 service. It also reads the error message returned by CAP and displays it using MessageStrip and MessageToast.
This is How I have written in controller.js file

sap.ui.define([
    "sap/ui/core/mvc/Controller",
    "sap/m/MessageToast"
], function (Controller, MessageToast) {
    "use strict";

    var SERVICE_URL = "/odata/v4/employee";

    return Controller.extend("project1.controller.View1", {

        _showResult: function (ok, message) {
            var oStrip = this.byId("resultStrip");
            oStrip.setType(ok ? "Success" : "Error");
            oStrip.setText(message);
            MessageToast.show(message);
        },

        _callService: function (method, path, body, onSuccessMessage) {
            var that = this;
            var options = { method: method, headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" } };
            if (body !== undefined) { options.body = JSON.stringify(body); }

            return fetch(SERVICE_URL + path, options)
                .then(function (response) {
                    return response.json().then(function (data) {
                        return { ok: response.ok, data: data };
                    });
                })
                .then(function (result) {
                    if (result.ok) {
                        var msg;
                        if (typeof onSuccessMessage === "function") {
                            msg = onSuccessMessage(result.data);
                        } else if (typeof result.data.value === "string") {
                            msg = result.data.value;
                        } else if (result.data.value !== undefined) {
                            msg = String(result.data.value);
                        } else {
                            msg = "Request succeeded";
                        }
                        that._showResult(true, msg);
                    } else {
                        var errMsg = (result.data.error && result.data.error.message) || "Request failed";
                        that._showResult(false, errMsg);
                    }
                })
                .catch(function (err) {
                    that._showResult(false, "Network / unexpected error: " + err.message);
                });
        },

        onCreateEmployee: function () {
            var newId = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) % 100000; // simple auto-generated ID
            var name = this.byId("nameInput").getValue();
            var email = this.byId("emailInput").getValue();
            var salary = this.byId("salaryInput").getValue();

            this._callService("POST", "/Employees", {
                ID: newId,
                name: name || undefined,
                email: email || undefined,
                salary: salary ? Number(salary) : undefined
            }, function (data) {
                return "Employee created: " + data.name + " (ID " + data.ID + ")";
            });
        },

        onGetEmployee: function () {
            var id = parseInt(this.byId("opIdInput").getValue(), 10) || 0;
            this._callService("POST", "/getEmployee", { ID: id });
        },

        onCalculateBonus: function () {
            var id = parseInt(this.byId("opIdInput").getValue(), 10) || 0;
            this._callService("POST", "/calculateBonus", { ID: id }, function (data) {
                return "Bonus: " + data.value;
            });
        }
    });
});

Step 10 – Run the Application

Start the CAP application from the project terminal:

cds watch

After the application starts, open the generated application URL and open the SAPUI5 application.

Note: For this blog, I am demonstrating the error handling through the SAPUI5 screen. Postman is not compulsory for this example.

Here is the Out of My Application

Step 11 – Test req.error()

To test validation, leave the Email field empty and click Create Employee.

Expected result:

  1. CAP receives the CREATE request.
  2. The before CREATE handler checks the email.
  3. req.error() adds the validation error.
  4. The UI displays the returned error message.

    Step 12 – Test req.reject() for Duplicate Email

    First create an employee with a valid email. Then try to create another employee using the same email.

    Expected result: the backend checks the existing employee and rejects the second request with HTTP 409.

     

    Step 13 – Test req.reject() for Employee Not Found

    Enter an employee ID that does not exist and click Get Employee.

    The getEmployee action searches the database. If no employee is found, req.reject(404, 'Employee not found') is executed.

     

    Step 14 – Test a Successful Request

    To show that the service also works for valid requests, enter valid employee details and create the employee.

     

You can also enter the newly created ID and click Calculate Bonus. For example, if the salary is 34,000, a 10% bonus is 3,400.

req.error() vs req.reject()

Feature

req.error()

req.reject()

Purpose

Report a validation error

Stop the request and reject it

Typical use

Field/business validation

Not found, conflict, unauthorized or other request-level errors

Example

Email is required

Employee not found

Example status

400

404 / 409 / other suitable status

In simple terms: use req.error() when you want to report validation problems during request processing, and use req.reject() when the request cannot continue and should be rejected.

Common Issues While Testing

  • Make sure the CAP server is running before calling the service.
  • Use the correct service path: /odata/v4/employee.
  • Check the action names: getEmployee and calculateBonus.
  • If you are using curl, run the command separately and make sure the URL does not contain terminal prompt text.
  • If you are testing through the UI, check the browser console if the application shows a network error.
  • After changing service.js, restart cds watch if the change is not reflected.

Conclusion

In this blog, we implemented simple error handling in a SAP CAPM application using a practical Employee example.

We covered:

  • req.error() for validation errors.
  • req.reject() for request-level errors such as employee not found and duplicate email.
  • try/catch for handling unexpected exceptions.
  • A global error handler for logging errors.
  • A SAPUI5 screen to test the backend error messages.

Good error handling makes the application easier to use and also makes troubleshooting easier for developers. Instead of showing a generic failure, we can return a clear message that explains what went wrong.

The same approach can be extended to real business scenarios such as customer validation, order processing, duplicate records, authorization checks and other business rules.

I hope this practical example helps you understand error handling in SAP CAPM.
Thank You

entry.title: SAP FSA Business Rules: Practical Examples to Avoid a Business Rule Jungle
entry.content:
SAP FSA Business Rules: Practical Examples to Avoid a Business Rule Jungle

Introduction

 
Business Rules (BRs) are the automation backbone of many SAP FSM implementations — they handle checklist attachment, field updates, notifications, etcetera, etcetera. The configuration decisions around business rules determine whether a system stays maintainable at scale or turns into a support burden.
 
Four anti-patterns - or bad examples - come up repeatedly across our engagements. We present them here with explanations why these patterns are suboptimal, and give recommendations of what we consider to be a better approach.
 

Anti-Pattern 1: One Trigger, Ten Rules

 
The situation: A client needs 10 different checklists attached when an Activity status changes to Released.
 
The mistake: Create 10 separate Business Rules, each targeting the same event, each attaching a different checklist.
 
What actually goes wrong: Ten rules on the same trigger means ten entries in the execution log every time an Activity is released. 9 Rules are triggered, leading to resource consumption, but ultimately skipped because conditions are not met. The total number of business rules explodes. When a checklist fails to attach in production, you trace through 10 rules to find which one was responsible. The BR landscape becomes more difficult to understand, monitor, and maintain.
 
What we recommend instead:
Combine all 10 into a single BR. Use JavaScript variables  to evaluate which checklist applies in each case and drive the Conditions and Actions from that output — use that capacity rather than splitting logic across multiple rules.
If you must use multiple rules, set the execution order to maintain control over the sequence of BR execution.
 

Anti-Pattern 2: Multiple Rules Updating the Same Record

 
The situation: Several conditions each require an update to the same ServiceCall record. Each condition gets its own BR firing on the same trigger.
 
The mistake: Ten BRs (or one BR with ten separate Actions) each writing a different field on the same record.
 
The problem with this approach: SAP FSM processes each write operation as an independent record update.  Therefore, having many separate business rules or actions update the same record can lead toa lot of data traffic, which scales poorly:
  • 10 BRs updating the same object → 10 DB record updates → 10x integration sync traffic
  • 1 BR with 10 Actions updating the same object  → same result: 10 DB record updates and 10x integration sync traffic
  • 1 BR with 1 Action updating multiple fields of one object at once → 1 DB record update → 1x integration sync traffic
What actually goes wrong: Multiple BRs fire within milliseconds of each other on the same record. This may cause many different issues: data race problems, sync conflicts, overwriting previous updates, update loops, triggering other BRs, etc. On top of this, it fills the audit logs with entries, so diagnosing problems becomes more difficult as well.
 
What we recommend instead: 
Consolidate field updates into a single Action. Use JavaScript to evaluate all conditions and determine which fields need changing, then write them in one Action. If no field change is needed, set the existing/old value as the new value. This cuts backend traffic, eliminates update loops, and keeps the audit log readable.
If you must use multiple BRs to update the same record or the same record type, add a UDF on the relevant object type (e.g. `Activity_LastUpdatedByBR`) and use Javascript to have each BR stamp it with the BR code and a timestamp, e.g. `BR042_2026-05-20T18:02:40Z` — this creates a more traceable audit trail.
 

Anti-Pattern 3: Many Rules, Same Event

 
The situation: An Activity release needs to trigger 10 downstream actions — field updates, notifications, checklist attachments, status changes on related objects.
 
The mistake: Create 10 Business Rules and move on.
 
What actually goes wrong: Having 10 rules on the same trigger results in confusion what is happening when and in which sequence. New requirements get added on top in a new BR out of inability to see through the complexity. A consultant adding or modifying one rule six months later breaks three others they didn't know existed.
 
What we recommend instead:
Consolidate the actions into as few BRs as reasonably possible. If there are slight variations in the conditions for an individual action, use the "Execute Conditional Operation" action to define whether a subsequent action should be executed or skipped. Again, if multiple rules are necessary, set an Execution Order on rules that share a trigger so the behavior is deterministic.
 

Anti-Pattern 4: Complex Trigger Condition Sets

 
The situation: A BR needs to fire only when a combination of five parameters aligns, in several possible valid combinations. You model this in the Trigger conditions panel.
 
The mistake: Build 10 condition sets, each checking a different combination of parameters directly in the trigger configuration.
 
The problem with this approach: The business rule conditions panel supports only simple evaluations. It doesn't support complex javascript with the condition itself. Ten multi-parameter condition sets stacked there produce something no one understands at a glance, and testing becomes difficult.
 
What we recommend instead: 
Move the logic into one or a few JavaScript variables, like `myCondition`. The variable evaluates all conditions and outputs a simple string — `condition_met` or `condition_not_met`. The trigger condition then checks: `${myCondition} == 'condition_met'`. The condition panel stays clean. The logic lives in JavaScript you can more easily test independently. When the condition changes you edit one variable, not ten condition rows.
 

Conclusion: Map Before You Configure

 
Before writing the first Business Rule on a new project, map the full intended BR scope, along the business process. This could be as a list or even as a graphical representation. List the triggers, actions, and objects involved. Group by trigger type and highlight overlaps. Then, carefully consider how to group conditions and actions into your business rules. When when building the individual business rules, give a thought to the best practices for business rules and find a balance between code complexity and readability of the overall business rule. This will help keep your BR landscape manageable.

 

If you are reviewing an existing implementation, run it against these four anti-patterns. A system where every requirement got its own BR is recoverable - but the refactoring cost grows with every new rule added on top.

Introduction:

If you already know what SAP Document AI is and want to see a practical integration example, this blog is for you.

For a full functional introduction, read my previous post:  SAP Document AI: Extracting Information from Documents.

In short, SAP Document AI automatically extracts structured information from business documents such as invoices and purchase orders. But knowing how it works in theory is one thing. Getting it to work reliably in a real BPA workflow is another.

In this post, I'll walk you through a practical integration—complete with what went wrong on my first attempt, which document types surprised me, and most importantly, proof that the workflow actually delivers value.

Prerequisites

Before you start, make sure you have:

  • Access to SAP BTP with the Document AI service enabled.
  • (Optional) Access to SAP Build Process Automation.
  • The necessary roles/permissions to call APIs and manage BPA projects.
Step 1: Get a Bearer Token

To call the Document AI API, you need an OAuth Bearer token.
If you’re using a configured destination in SAP BTP, you can skip this step.

Otherwise, use the following API call to get your token:

return{
    method:'GET',
    url:docurl + '/oauth/token?grant_type=client_credentials',
    responseType : 'JSON',
    resolveBodyOnly: true,
    headers: {
        Authorization: 'Basic ' + <Encoded_clientCredentials>
    },
 }

 

Tip : Encode your client ID and client secret as `client_id:client_secret` in Binary for the Authorization header.
 Step 2: Submit Your Document for Extraction

Now, you need to tell Document AI what kind of document you’re sending and which schema to use.
This is done by setting the right metadata in your request.

let documentOption = {
documentType: "custom", // or "invoice", "purchaseOrder", etc.
schemaName: "SAP_invoice_schema",
headerFields: ["purchaseOrderNumber"],
clientId: "default"
};

let payloadDocAICall = {
method: 'POST',
url: <url> + "/document-information-extraction/v1/document/jobs",
responseType: "json",
resolveBodyOnly: true,
metadataType: irpa_core.enums.request.metadataType.formData,
headers: {
Authorization: <access_token>
},
metadata: [
{
name: "file",
file: <filePath>,
},
{
name: "options",
value: JSON.stringify(documentOption)
}
],
timeout: 30000
};
return payloadDocAICall;

 

  • documentType: The type of document (e.g., "invoice", "custom")
  • schemaName: The schema you defined in Document AI

Step 3: Check the Job Status

After submitting your document, you’ll get a job ID.
You need to check the status of this job to see if extraction is complete.

let option = {
method: 'GET',
url: docAiUrl + "/document-information-extraction/v1/document/jobs/" + <your_job-id>,
responseType: "json",
resolveBodyOnly: true,
headers: {
Authorization: <your_token>,
'Cache-Control': 'no-cache'
}
};
return option;
Step 4: Poll Until the Job is Done

In your BPA workflow, use a forever loop (or a repeat-until loop) to keep checking the job status.

  • If the status is `"DONE"`, exit the loop and process the results.
  • If the status is `"PENDING"` or `"RUNNING"`, wait a few seconds and check again.

This ensures you only move forward once the extraction is complete.

Step 5: Process the Extracted Data

Once your job status is `"DONE"`, you can access the extracted fields in the response and use them in your workflow.

Error Handling
  • Always check for errors in API responses (e.g., invalid token, file not found, extraction failed).
  • If the job status returns `"FAILED"`, log the error and notify the user or take corrective action.
  • Handle timeouts and network issues gracefully by retrying or alerting the user.
Real-World Use Case

Imagine you receive 200 vendor invoices every month:

Phase 1 (Manual Entry):

  • 60 hours/month on data entry
  • 8% error rate = 16 invoices with mistakes

Phase 2 (With SAP Document AI):

  • Configure schema, test on 10 documents
  • Deploy to production with 80% confidence threshold
  • Monitor, tweak thresholds, handle edge cases

  • Loop: Check Status (GET job status until "DONE")

Note: The output can vary significantly depending on the invoice format, layout, and document quality. In my experience, the same schema did not always produce the same level of accuracy across all invoice variants. Some documents returned clean, structured fields immediately, while others required additional testing, schema refinements, or validation logic to capture all required information correctly. For this reason, it is important to test with multiple document formats and real-world examples before moving the workflow to production.

Conclusion

With this approach, you can automate document data extraction in SAP Build Process Automation using SAP Document AI from end to end.

Instead of manual data entry, your process can:

  1. Submit documents for extraction
  2. Poll job status until completion
  3. Consume structured output automatically
  4. Trigger business actions with minimal human effort

This pattern is especially useful for high-volume document scenarios such as invoice intake and validation.

entry.title: Update on SAPUI5 / OpenUI5 2.x: Best-Practice Code Is Your Best Strategy
entry.content:
In late 2023, we introduced OpenUI5 2.x with a clear goal: renew the UI5 framework by removing deprecated libraries and functionality, making it leaner, faster, and future-proof. Since then, the UI5 team has made significant progress towards this legacy-free vision — from cleaning up the core to providing tooling that helps you modernize your applications. This post is an update on where we stand with SAPUI5 / OpenUI5 2.x and what it means for you.

 

SAPUI5 / OpenUI5 2.x delivery is on hold

UI5 2.x is currently on hold from a delivery perspective. The technical work is largely done. We have cleaned up the framework, removed synchronous APIs, eliminated globals, and followed internally the same rules we ask you to follow externally. The migration tooling achieves a very high percentage of automatic conversion rates for application code. From a pure readiness standpoint, we could ship.

However, the rapid evolution of AI has fundamentally changed the questions we need to answer. What does the future programming model look like for an AI-native user experience? How should application design evolve? How do we best address the challenges and opportunities that AI brings to UI development? UI5 2.x is legacy-free, and that has clear advantages — but it is not fundamentally different from the current stack. From an AI perspective, it would not solve additional problems compared to what UI5 1.x already provides today. If we want to bring something genuinely new, addressing different problems, we likely need to do more than what version 2.x set out to do.

We have therefore decided to put the delivery on hold and use this opportunity to explore how the UI5 framework can be positioned to play a best-in-class role in an AI-driven environment.

SAPUI5 remains SAP's strategic UI technology for building applications. We want to make sure it continues to play a key role in the AI age.

The foundational work pays off

While the delivery of SAPUI5 2.x as a separate version is on hold, the foundational work we have done is far from wasted — it is already paying off today.

  • Legacy-free cleanup across the stack. We have cleaned up the UI5 core, synchronous module loading (to the extent possible in a compatible way) and globals, and deprecating non-compliant APIs. The basic UI5 libraries are legacy-free, the SAP Fiori launchpad provides a new sandbox with async services, and the SAP Fiori elements cleanup is underway.
  • UI5 linter. With a single command, you get an audit of your application that that tells you what needs to be corrected to comply with UI5 best practices. The linter also includes an autofix capability for deterministic fixes.
  • UI5 Modernization AI skills. What the linter cannot fix automatically, AI takes further. The UI5 Modernization Plugin for coding agents (e.g. for Claude Code or GitHub Copilot) run the linter, scan for solutions, and execute code changes to clean up your codebase. Together with the UI5 Linter autofix option, this achieves a very high percentage of automated migrations to legacy-free best practices. While manual testing is still required, we continue to close the remaining gaps.

These tools and the cleaned-up codebase benefit you regardless of how the UI5 versioning evolves. Following UI5 best practices — TypeScript first, asynchronous loading, no globals — makes your applications better, future-proof and ready for what comes next.

What you should do

The message is clear: keep modernizing your applications. The foundational work towards legacy-free is valuable today and will carry forward.

  1. Follow UI5 best practices: TypeScript first, asynchronous loading, no globals, no deprecated APIs.
  2. Use the UI5 linter to audit your applications against UI5 best practices.
  3. Use the UI5 Modernization Plugin with your coding agent to automate the migration to best-practice-compliant code.

Everything you do to modernize your applications today benefits you now — cleaner code, better performance, improved security, easier updates — and prepares you for the future.

Stay informed

This blog post is the official communication channel for updates on SAPUI5 / OpenUI5 2.x. When there is news to share, the UI5 team will add updates here. Subscribing to this blog post is sufficient to stay informed.
